一句话：压缩让训练可行，却同时锁死了分辨率、控制粒度与交互延迟。

要点：

  • 成本账算得很清楚：潜空间把视频在空间与时间上同时压缩，分辨率翻倍就是 token 数翻四倍；条件只能作用于**一组帧**而不是单帧；每次响应都要等这一整组多帧算完
  • PixVid 的做法是保留扩散 transformer，把 **VAE 解码器换成一个卷积头**，直接在像素空间逐帧生成
  • 换句话说，它把「压缩带来的可控性与延迟损失」用输出端的渲染头补回来，而不是退回重训一个像素空间的大模型

为什么值得看：「交互式生成」的瓶颈常常不在模型能力，而在表示：只要条件粒度是「一组帧」，就无法做逐帧响应。这条把约束定位到 VAE 的时空压缩上，并给出一个不重训主干就能改的方案——对要做实时可控生成的管线是很直接的路径。

中文摘要：前沿视频生成模型工作在 VAE 潜空间里，潜空间在空间与时间两个维度同时压缩。这种压缩让训练变得可行，但现在反过来限制了高分辨率、可控与交互式生成：分辨率翻倍会让 token 数变成四倍；条件只能作用在一组帧上而不是单帧；每一次响应都必须等整组多帧全部算完。PixVid 提出把预训练的潜空间视频模型「提到」像素空间——保留扩散 transformer，只把 VAE 解码器换成一个卷积头，让模型直接逐帧生成像素。这样既不重训主干，又把可控粒度从「帧组」拉回到「单帧」，同时切掉了块内等待。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-15

Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space

Abstract

Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation – doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within ∼1.3M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at 2× higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

1 Introduction

Early video diffusion models [32, 30] generated videos in their native form, as sequences of pixel frames. As models scaled up, the field made two shifts away from pixel space: The first followed latent diffusion [72], moving generation into the latent space of a pretrained variational autoencoder (VAE) [48], initially with one latent per frame [7, 6]. The second extended the compression to time, using 3D VAEs to merge every few frames into a single latent that corresponds to no individual frame [93, 85]. For generating short clips offline at moderate resolution, this was a favorable trade: compression made training tractable at scale, at the cost of a frozen VAE that ruled out end-to-end training and capped quality at its reconstruction [14, 23, 77].

Video generation models have since outgrown this setting: they now power real-time interactive world models [27, 79, 33] through causal few-step distillation [97, 38], and serve as geometry-conditioned renderers for editing and games [43, 62, 63]. Yet these systems inherit the VAE’s fixed compression in space and time, which works against each new demand. Under a real-time compute budget, doubling the resolution yields 4× more tokens and 16× more attention compute, while cutting tokens requires a more aggressive VAE that further reduces quality. Precise editing requires conditions aligned to individual frames, but when several frames share one latent, fast motion blurs and objects deform (Fig. 5). Temporal compression also limits responsiveness. Since common latent world models [97, 38, 92, 27, 79, 37] autoregressively generate frames in blocks, the frame corresponding to a control cannot be generated until all controls for the full block are received. This results in a minimum control-to-screen latency proportional to the block size, a barrier that no model-side optimization can remove.

These limitations motivate removing the VAE altogether and generating every frame directly as pixels, which naively would bring back the token counts and training costs that latent models avoid. Recent pixel-space image models overcome both challenges [50, 98, 19, 18, 41, 13] by modeling semantics over large pixel patches [50] and delegating fine details to a lightweight decoder [19], thus keeping the token count and training cost reasonable. Moreover, although training video models from scratch demands prohibitive data and compute resources, a pretrained latent model already captures high-level semantics and dynamics. Hence, finetuning it into a pixel space video model only requires changing the output interface, which is a more feasible task.

In this work, we present PixVid, a recipe that lifts a pretrained latent video diffusion model into a frame-wise pixel-space model, in which every token covers a 1×p×p patch of exactly one frame, so no condition or action spans multiple frames. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer (DiT) and replaces both the encoder and the decoder from the VAE (Fig. 2). At input, a patch embedding that initializes from the VAE encoder allows the DiT to start training from close to its pretrained latent distribution. At output, a lightweight detailer head renders the DiT tokens into pixels; it is convolutional to suppress the patch-grid artifacts of a linear head [88], and causal in time to allow autoregressive generation. We further identify the following key techniques: 1) predicting clean video (x-prediction) rather than velocity, since velocity prediction forces the network to model full-rank per-pixel noise [50]; 2) using a larger noise shift, since redundant pixels retain more signal at the same noise level; and 3) using the Euler sampler, since pixel color values are numerically sensitive to higher order solvers like UniPC [101].

Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B [85], PixVid converges within 1.3M training clips sampled from 64K videos, or about 4K B200 GPU-hours. It achieves competitive quality with the original latent model on VBench [39], and the recipe transfers across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2-based models with different VAEs. Generating frame by frame in pixels, it introduces several benefits, as shown in Fig.1. Resolution: doubling the patch size lets PixVid generate 960×1664 with the same number of tokens per frame as at 480×832. Control: with the same control branch as the latent model, depth-conditioned editing keeps 98% of the source’s fast motion, versus 83% for an identically finetuned latent model. Latency: after autoregressive distillation, each camera control takes effect at the next frame rather than the next block, cutting median latency from 495 ms to 34 ms while still streaming in real time.

To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose PixVid, a recipe that lifts a pretrained latent video diffusion model into a frame-wise pixel-space model, converging quickly to competitive quality.

  • •

    We identify the design choices that make this lift work: a causal convolutional detailer head with 9× fewer patch seams than a linear head, x-prediction with 80× less pixel noise than v-prediction, and a larger noise shift than the latent model.

  • •

    We show frame-wise pixel generation overcomes three structural limitations of latent models: resolution scaling, control alignment under fast motion, and control-to-screen latency.

    • 2 Related Work

    Pixel-Space Diffusion. Latent diffusion [72, 68, 7] has been favored for efficient training using spatial and temporal compression for video [93, 85, 8], at the price of a VAE reconstruction bottleneck. Pixel-space diffusion models for images [29, 78, 22, 46] and videos [32, 30, 76, 5] bypass a VAE but become costly at high resolution, historically requiring cascaded or multi-resolution designs [31, 74, 71, 26, 20, 81]. Recent methods improved pixel-space image generation, training from scratch [34, 35, 15, 50, 98, 19, 58, 87, 55, 57, 13, 61] or finetuning from latent checkpoints to make training tenable [18, 41, 13]. Pixel-space video generation is less explored. Concurrent works train from scratch, and they either focus on smaller class-conditioned benchmarks [84] or have undesirable patch artifacts [88]. We finetune a pretrained latent video model, inheriting its prior capabilities and maintaining competitive quality.

    Controllable Video Generation and Editing. Early video editors applied image diffusion models with heuristics such as cross-frame shared self-attention [89, 70, 47, 24] or propagated edits [4, 91, 67]. Video diffusion models improve consistency and robustness, with recent models producing precise, aligned edits and structure-guided generation [43, 94, 45, 62, 49, 73, 10, 25].

    Interactive Video Generation. Interactive generation produces frames as a stream, typically with autoregressive video diffusion models [11, 21, 90, 80, 12]. Combined with few-step distillation [96, 95, 97, 38, 92, 104, 17], latent world models respond to user actions across diverse scenes in real time [27, 60, 79, 33], but temporal compression delays each action, e.g. by up to three frames for Wan’s four-frame latents [85]. Per-frame latent [9, 83] and pixel-space [2, 65] world models avoid this delay but are trained from scratch on a single genre. PixVid is finetuned from a general pretrained model and responds to actions at the next frame.

    3 Methods

    Our goal is to generate every frame directly in pixels without training a pixel-space video model from scratch, while removing the VAE bottleneck. PixVid achieves this by lifting a pretrained latent video diffusion model into a frame-wise pixel-space model, as shown in Fig. 2. We describe its architecture in Sec. 3.1 and how we train it from the latent model in Sec. 3.2, including key design choices. We then adapt it to efficient high-resolution generation in Sec. 3.3, precise video editing in Sec. 3.4, and low-latency autoregressive generation in Sec. 3.5.

    3.1 Architecture

    PixVid keeps the DiT [68] backbone of a pretrained latent video model and replaces the VAE: a linear patch embedding maps pixels to tokens, and a lightweight convolutional detailer head renders the DiT outputs directly into pixels.

    Frame-Wise Tokenization. Latent video models merge several frames into one latent [93, 85], so conditions apply to groups of frames. PixVid instead gives each frame its own tokens, each covering a 1×p×p pixel patch. Conditions then align with individual frames, and an autoregressive model can respond to actions at the next frame. Although this approach uses more tokens per clip than with temporal compression, the spatial token count does not grow with resolution as it is determined by the adjustable patch size rather than a frozen VAE.

    Detailer Head. Since the DiT captures global structure and leaves only local details to render, we implement the detailer as a lightweight 3D convolutional decoder, sharing this insight with pixel-space image models [19, 18, 41]. Unlike their U-Net detailers, which also encode the noisy pixels of each patch, ours keeps only the decoder path and reads only the DiT tokens. It stacks L=\log₂p up blocks, each upsampling by 1×2×2, so the head maps each token to a 1×p×p pixel patch and predicts the clean video. Its convolutions also run across neighboring tokens rather than within each patch, which largely suppresses checkerboard artifacts at token boundaries. They are causal in time, so the detailer models local temporal structure without reading future frames and supports frame-by-frame generation. See App. A.2 for details.

    3.2 Training from a Latent Model

    PixVid finetunes end-to-end in pixel space from a pretrained latent model, with initialized DiT and input patchification, x-prediction, a larger noise shift, and auxiliary losses.

    Initialization. To retain the pretrained latent model’s prior, we inherit its DiT weights and randomly initialize the detailer head. Following AsymFlow [13], we approximate the VAE encoder with a linear map A fitted offline between pixel patches and their latents, and compose it with the pretrained patch embedding to initialize the pixel patch embedding. We further employ an internal timestep calibration, with scale c estimated alongside A, to ensure the signal-to-noise ratios of latent and pixel spaces are aligned. The DiT thus initially receives inputs close to the latents it was trained on. Full details appear in App. A.1.

    x-Prediction. Under flow matching [53], a clean video x is corrupted with Gaussian noise ε∼ℕ(0,I) at noise level σ∈[0,1] as x_σ=(1-σ) x+σ ε. Following JiT [50], the network predicts the clean video x̂=x_θ(x_σ,σ), and we compute the flow matching loss in velocity space,

    L_flow=𝔼_x,ε,σ∥v̂-v∥₂²,

    		(1)

    where v̂=(x_σ-x̂)/\max(σ,σ_\min) and v=(x_σ-x)/\max(σ,σ_\min) are the predicted and target velocities, and σ_\min clips the denominator to avoid numerical instability at low noise levels. Latent models typically predict v while pixel-space image models either predict v[19, 18, 98] or switch to x[50, 41]. We find x-prediction essential for video, as it enables the detailer to render the DiT tokens into clean local structure that lies near a low-dimensional manifold [50]. Predicting v would instead require the network to model the full-rank per-pixel noise in x_σ, a burden that increases with patch size. Figure 9 shows v-prediction fills the video with high-frequency, flickering noise.

    Auxiliary Losses. The temporal convolutions of the detailer are trained from scratch, so we add a loss on frame differences to learn temporal smoothness,

    Lₜₑₘₚ=𝔼_x,ε,σ ρ(Δx̂-Δx),

    		(2)

    where Δx^(f)=x^(f+1)-x^(f) is the difference between consecutive frames f and f+1, and ρ(u)=√u²+δ² is the Charbonnier penalty with a small constant δ, averaged over all elements. We also add an LPIPS perceptual loss [99] on x̂, which improves the visual quality of pixel-space image models [59]. Both losses are weighted toward low noise levels, where x̂ is informative. The total loss is thus

    L=L_flow+λₜₑₘₚ Lₜₑₘₚ+λ_LPIPS L_LPIPS,

    		(3)

    where λₜₑₘₚ and λ_LPIPS are loss weights.

    3.3 Efficient High-Resolution Generation

    The high-level semantic content of a video changes little with resolution, so higher resolution should mainly require finer rendering, not more tokens. A latent DiT cannot exploit this, as doubling the resolution yields 4× more latent tokens. PixVid instead doubles the patch size from p to 2p and adds one up block to the detailer, keeping the token grid unchanged (Fig. 3). Unlike PixelDiT [98], whose token count grows with resolution, or DiP [19] and L2P [18], which add no detailer levels, this gives the doubled resolution its own upsampling level without much additional cost.

    We finetune the patch-2p model from the patch-p model. Its patch embedding fuses 2×2 average pooling with the patch-p embedding, so the DiT initially sees a downsampled version of its input, and the new upsampling block starts as an identity pass-through, acting as nearest-neighbor upsampling. We also double both the calibration scale and the noise shift [23], so the DiT sees the same noise schedule as at patch p. See App. A.3 for details.

    3.4 Precise Video Editing

    Precise video editing, such as re-rendering a video from its per-frame depth, requires the generated video to align with the condition at every frame. Latent models typically encode the condition with the same VAE as the video [43], so several condition frames share one latent, leading to inaccurate alignment, especially in fast motions. In PixVid, the condition is tokenized per frame as the corresponding video, so generation and condition are aligned at the frame level, without changing the conditioning mechanism. Concretely, we add the control branch of VACE [43]: conditions are residually added to the DiT tokens via control blocks, and the condition’s patch embedding is initialized, like the video’s, by fusing the pretrained embedding with A.

    3.5 Low-Latency Autoregressive Generation

    Interactive applications stream video in response to user controls, such as camera or motion inputs, and should react to each control as soon as it arrives. An autoregressive model generates video in blocks, and a block can start only once the controls for all its frames have arrived. In a temporally compressed latent model, each block spans at least one latent, i.e., several frames, so a new control waits for the rest of its block, a delay that no throughput-side optimization can remove (Fig. 6). PixVid can generate single-frame blocks, so each control takes effect at the next frame. To achieve this, we lift a bidirectional latent model to pixel space with the recipe above and distill it into a few-step causal model with Self Forcing [38]. The causal detailer decodes one frame at a time from cached features of previous frames, keeping its cost per frame constant. Single-frame blocks trade some throughput for this latency gain, which we analyze in Sec. 4.5.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate PixVid on text-to-video generation in Sec. 4.2, followed by its three applications: efficient high-resolution generation in Sec. 4.3, precise video editing in Sec. 4.4, and low-latency autoregressive generation in Sec. 4.5. Finally, we ablate our key design choices in Sec. 4.6.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    We lift three pretrained latent models into pixel space: Wan2.1-T2V-14B [85] for text-to-video and high-resolution generation, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B for video editing and ablations, and the camera-controlled SolarWM-5B [37] for interactive generation. Unless otherwise noted, models generate 21-frame videos with patch size p=16 and sample with 50 Euler steps at the training shift. Each experiment below gives its key setup. Full details are in App. B.

    4.2 Text-to-Video Generation

    Setup. We finetune Wan2.1-T2V-14B [85] into a frame-wise pixel-space model at 480×832 for 20K iterations, on 64K videos generated by Wan2.1. We use shift s=11, which gives the DiT nearly the same effective shift as the best 1.3B setting (Sec. 4.6). We evaluate on VBench [39] with its 946 GPT-enhanced prompts and five videos per prompt, and run a pairwise human study on 100 random prompts from Movie Gen Video Bench [69] comparing visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment. We compare against our base latent model, Wan2.1-T2V-14B, and the concurrent pixel-space model PixelUMM [88] using their official settings (App. B.2). Since our models generate 21 frames, we score every model on the first 1.3 s of each video, which has no meaningful impact compared to scoring full videos in Tab.6.

    Results. In Tab.1, PixVid reaches a VBench total of 84.78, above both Wan2.1 (84.05) and PixelUMM (83.72). Replacing the VAE decoder with the detailer head does not cost visual quality: imaging quality, aesthetic quality, and dynamic degree improve over Wan2.1, while consistency and smoothness stay within 1.4 points. PixVid also achieves the highest semantic score of 82.15; color is the only semantic dimension where it trails Wan2.1 by more than a point (81.59 vs. 84.73). In the human study in Fig.4, raters prefer PixVid across all comparisons, showing that finetuning is competitive with the pretrained latent model and compares favorably with PixelUMM, which is trained from scratch.

    4.3 Efficient High-Resolution Generation

    Setup. We generate 960×1664 videos with the same 30×52 token grid per frame as 480×832 generation by doubling the patch size from 16 to 32. We first train a patch-16 pixel model at 480×832, then finetune it at 960×1664 with patch 32 with twice the shift and an additional scale-2 calibration. We train on 40K synthetic videos resized and cropped to the training resolution, and evaluate with the same VBench protocol as Sec.4.2.

    Results. Using the same number of tokens per frame as 480p, the 960×1664 model reaches the highest VBench total of 85.09 and the best imaging, aesthetic, background-consistency, and temporal-flickering scores in Tab.1. Its semantic score of 80.68 is below the 480×832 model’s, mostly in color. Doubling the patch size therefore keeps PixVid competitive at 4 times the pixels per frame. Its cost per clip stays close to a latent model’s at this resolution: a 21-frame clip has 32,760 tokens and takes 192 s on one B200, against 37,440 tokens and 176 s for a Wan2.1-VAE latent model (App. B.7). Since VBench resizes frames to at most 512 pixels before scoring, it does not measure the added detail, which we show in Fig. 1(a).

    4.4 Precise Video Editing

    Setup. We add the control branch of VACE [43] to PixVid-1.3B and finetune it to re-render a video from its per-frame depth and a caption. We compare with VACE-1.3B, finetuned with the same control branch, data, and training settings; and with off-the-shelf depth-conditioned models without finetuning. We train on 79K stock videos with varied camera and object motion and paired depth [16], and evaluate on 1,000 held-out clips across alignment, temporal fidelity, and video quality. Alignment is measured by optical flow error, the fraction of source motion kept, and depth error, while temporal fidelity and video quality are measured by temporal LPIPS, FVMD [54], and FVD [82]. Fast clips are the quarter with the most motion; details are in App. B.4.

    Results. PixVid keeps the scene intact under fast motion, where the latent model morphs and blurs moving objects (Fig. 5). On fast clips, it lowers motion error by 40% and depth error by 20%, and keeps 98% of the source motion, against 83% for the finetuned latent model and at most 63% for the zero-shot models (Tab.2). It also has the lowest FVMD and tLP and leads on all four per-clip metrics over all 1,000 clips (Tab.7), while its FVD trails (118 vs. 91).

    4.5 Low-Latency Autoregressive Generation

    Setup. We lift the bidirectional SolarWM-5B base [37] into pixel space and distill it with Self Forcing [38] into a 4-step causal student that generates one frame per block. We compare with the official causal student distilled from the same base, referred to as SolarWM, which generates blocks of 12 frames (3 latents). We evaluate quality and camera following on camera paths from nine public datasets, and responsiveness on abrupt turns, measuring how closely the generated motion follows each control (App. B.5). We measure control-to-screen latency, which includes both the wait for controls from the same block and the model’s generation time. We time both models on one B200 GPU with the same kernels.

    Results. PixVid cuts median control-to-screen latency from 495 ms to 34 ms (Tab.3). Most of SolarWM’s latency is waiting for controls from the same 12-frame block, so at 16 fps a control waits up to 688 ms before generation even begins. A one-latent block would still wait 3 frames, and our experiments find finetuning SolarWM to one-latent blocks hurts performance (App. B.5). Frame-wise generation lowers throughput, since every frame has its own tokens: PixVid needs about 3× SolarWM’s DiT FLOPs per frame and runs at 29.4 vs. 72.0 fps, but both models exceed their base Wan model’s native 16 fps, so both stream in real time. SolarWM’s extra throughput cannot shorten its control-to-screen latency.

    PixVid follows abrupt turns more closely (Turn 0.95 vs. 0.70; Fig.7), since it receives a camera pose for every frame, whereas SolarWM receives one per four-frame latent. Its FVD is comparable to SolarWM’s (51.1 vs. 53.8), while its camera rotation and translation errors are higher (5.44^∘ vs. 4.24^∘ and 0.312 vs. 0.231). This is likely due to drift accumulated over a longer sequence of poses. Indeed, at 21 frames our errors are comparable to SolarWM’s (Tab.9). Mitigating such drift is an active area of research, so we leave it to future work.

    4.6 Ablation Study

    Setup. All ablations finetune Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B for 10K iterations and change one design choice at a time from our final recipe: the convolutional head, x-prediction, and shift. We generate one video for each of 119 VBench prompts and measure the artifact that each choice targets using three reference-free metrics defined in App. B.6: Seam, discontinuities along the patch grid; Noise, the per-pixel noise level; and Flicker, noise that changes from frame to frame. The noise shift decides how training and sampling are spread across noise levels, which affects global structure as well as local noise, so we score the shift sweep on VBench, with all 946 prompts and one video per prompt.

    Results.Output head. A linear head maps each DiT token to its pixel patch independently, so the head itself does not make neighboring patches agree at their borders, and the patch grid stays visible (Fig. 8). Our convolutional head, whose kernels span patch borders, lowers the seam measure from 118.6 to 13.3. The U-Net head, which additionally encodes the noisy input, reaches a similar seam (9.2) with slightly higher noise (0.848 vs. 0.777) and flicker (0.429 vs. 0.406), and it has 5.6× more parameters (248M vs. 44M at 1.3B), so we use the decoder-only head.

    Prediction target. As shown in Fig.9, v-prediction with our head fills the video with flickering high-frequency noise at 80 times the noise level of x-prediction, because predicting velocity requires the network to reproduce the per-pixel noise of its input. Asymmetric v-prediction [13] reduces the seams of the linear head (24.5 vs. 118.6), but its linear recovery rule still leaves nearly twice the seams of our head, and the noisy input it reads raises noise and flicker (0.897 and 0.524) above those of x-prediction.

    Noise shift. Since pixels are more redundant than latents, the SNR-aligned timestep calibration in App. A.1 naturally dictates a higher shift for pixel models. Here we ablate the uncalibrated shift s.

    Table4 shows that VBench peaks at s=15 in both total and semantic score, with s=5 close behind in total (84.27 vs. 84.40), and declines at larger shifts, mostly in spatial relationship and multiple objects. We therefore use s=15, giving an effective shift of 3.97 under scale c=3.78. For the other models we keep a similar effective shift: s=11 for the 14B model gives an effective shift of 3.86 under c=2.85, and at 960×1664 we double both the shift and the calibration.

    Sampler. Latent video models, including Wan2.1, typically sample with UniPC [101], which works well with a bf16 sampler state in latent space. In pixel space, a bf16 state makes UniPC drain color, keeping only 91% of the fp32 chroma, whereas Euler keeps it without needing an fp32 state (Fig.10). We suspect pixel space colors are more sensitive to higher order samplers. We therefore use the Euler sampler and leave further analysis to future work.

    5 Conclusion

    Latent video diffusion models compress video in space and time with a VAE. PixVid removes this compression by efficiently finetuning a pretrained latent model to generate every frame directly in pixels, reaching quality competitive with the original model. Working frame by frame in pixels, it overcomes three structural limitations of latent models: resolution scaling, control alignment under fast motion, and control-to-screen latency.

    Limitations and future work. Without temporal compression, PixVid processes 3.9× as many tokens per second of video as Wan2.1 at 480×832, so short low-resolution clips cost more than with a latent model, although the gap closes at higher resolution and streaming stays faster than real time (App. B.7). Generating directly in pixels also opens up training options that a frozen VAE rules out. Losses and rewards can be defined on pixels, enabling adversarial training and RL with pixel-space rewards. Because all models then share the same output space, distillation across architectures or from mixed teachers also becomes possible.

    Acknowledgments. We thank Yicong Hong, Zhanpeng Luo, and Wei-An Lin for their assistance in human evaluation.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Architecture Details

    In this section, we show the model architecture details.

    A.1 Input Patch Embedding Initialization

    The pretrained DiT reads latent tokens through a linear patch embedding W, while PixVid reads pixel patches. Following AsymFlow [13], we bridge the two with a linear lift between latent tokens and pixel patches, compose it with W to initialize the pixel patch embedding, and calibrate the timestep so that the DiT initially receives inputs on the latent trajectory it was trained on.

    Pixel-Latent Alignment.

    Let x∈ℝ^3p² be a 1×p×p pixel patch in normalized OKLab, and z∈ℝᵈ the latent token at the same location, i.e., the VAE latent patchified by the DiT. For Wan2.1 [85], the 8× spatial VAE downsampling and the 1×2×2 DiT patch give p=16, so 3p²=768 and d=64. We approximate the VAE encoder by a linear lift x≈c Az, where A∈ℝ^3p²×d has orthonormal columns (A^⊤A=I_d) and c>0 is a scalar. Collecting N paired patches and tokens from 500 training clips into X∈ℝ^3p²×N and Z∈ℝ^d×N, we fit A by orthogonal Procrustes [75],

    A=\argmin_A^⊤A=I_d∥X-AZ∥_F²=UV^⊤,

    		(4)

    where XZ^⊤=UΣV^⊤ is the compact SVD. Procrustes matches directions but not magnitudes, so we set the scale by matching Frobenius norms,

    c=∥A^⊤X∥_F / ∥Z∥_F,

    		(5)

    which gives c=2.85 for Wan2.1-T2V-14B and c=3.78 for Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B.

    Patch Embedding.

    Since z≈A^⊤x/c, we initialize the pixel patch embedding as WA^⊤, with the bias copied from the pretrained embedding. The 1/c factor is absorbed into the input calibration below. Components of x outside the span of A are initially discarded, and the patch embedding is trained with the rest of the model to pick them up.

    Internal Timestep Calibration.

    Projecting a noisy pixel patch x_σ=(1-σ) x+σ ε onto the lift gives

    A^⊤x_σ≈c(1-σ) z+σ ε_z,

    		(6)

    where ε_z=A^⊤ε∼ℕ(0,I_d) stays standard Gaussian since A has orthonormal columns. Its signal-to-noise ratio is that of the latent flow at the noise level σ^′ satisfying (1-σ^′)/σ^′=c(1-σ)/σ, i.e.,

    σ^′=σ/c(1-σ)+σ.

    		(7)

    Rescaling the input by k(σ)=σ^′/σ=1/(c(1-σ)+σ) further matches the magnitude,

    k(σ) A^⊤x_σ≈(1-σ^′) z+σ^′ ε_z,

    		(8)

    which is a sample of the pretrained latent flow at noise level σ^′. We therefore feed the DiT the input k(σ) x_σ with timestep σ^′ throughout training and sampling. Since c>1, σ^′<σ: at the same σ, the redundant pixels carry more signal than the latents, and the calibration accounts for it by shifting the noise schedule seen by the DiT, as ablated in Sec.4.6. Unlike AsymFlow, which predicts velocity and inherits the pretrained output head through a calibrated output conversion, PixVid predicts x̂ with a newly initialized detailer, so no output calibration is needed.

    A.2 Detailer Head

    The detailer head replaces the linear output head and the VAE decoder of the pretrained latent model, mapping DiT features directly to pixels (Fig. 11). Its input is the last DiT hidden state s on the token grid of size H/p×W/p with width D. We add the timestep embedding eₜ to s, apply a SiLU, and project the result with a 3×1×1 bottleneck convolution. A stack of Up Blocks then upsamples the features to the full resolution H×W, and a final 3×1×1 convolution outputs the pixel prediction x̂. Since the head upsamples only spatially, it keeps the temporal resolution of the token grid. Each Up Block doubles the spatial resolution, so a 1×16×16 patch requires 4 Up Blocks, with widths C₄,…,C₁. We use D=1536 and C=[512,256,128,64] for the 1.3B model, and D=5120 and C=[1024,256,64,64] for the 14B model, giving detailer heads with 44M and 337M parameters, respectively.

    Up Block.

    Each Up Block applies a 1×2×2 transposed convolution to double the height and width, followed by a 3×3×3 causal convolution and a SiLU. The transposed convolution upsamples each frame independently, and the causal convolution mixes information spatially and across neighboring frames at the new resolution.

    Causal Decoding.

    All temporal kernels in the head have size 3 and are padded only on the past side, so at every layer output frame t depends only on input frames t-2, t-1, and t (Fig. 11, bottom right). Therefore, the head never reads future frames and is compatible with causal, frame-by-frame generation. When decoding a stream, each convolution caches its two most recent input frames, so every new frame is decoded at a constant cost without recomputing earlier frames.

    A.3 Detailer Head for Higher Resolution

    To generate 960×1664 videos, we double the patch size from 1×p×p to 1×2p×2p, so the token grid stays at 30×52 per frame while the resolution doubles. Table 5 compares the two detailer heads.

    Patch Embedding.

    The 1×2p×2p patch embedding is built from the pretrained 1×p×p one by repeating each weight over a 2×2 block and scaling by 1/4. This is exactly a 2×2 average pooling ℙ followed by the pretrained patch embedding, so at initialization the DiT sees a 480p-equivalent input.

    Timestep Calibration.

    Pooling keeps the signal but halves the standard deviation of the i.i.d. noise, so 2 ℙ(x_σ)\oversetd=2(1-σ) ℙ(x)+σ ε. This has the form of Eq. (6) with c=2, so we apply the calibration of App. A.1 with scale 2, i.e., timestep σ/(2-σ) and input 2/2-σ ℙ(x_σ), on top of the calibration of the patch-p model. Composing two calibrations multiplies their scales, so the DiT sees a single calibration of Eq. (7) with scale 2c. We also double the noise shift, which keeps the effective shift s/c unchanged, so the DiT sees the same noise schedule as the patch-p model.

    Appendix B Experiment Details

    B.1 Common Settings

    Videos are represented in the OKLab color space [66], with each channel normalized by its mean and standard deviation over the training data. Unless otherwise noted, models are trained with a global batch size of 64 on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

    We use AdamW [56] with β₁=0.9, β₂=0.95, and no weight decay, with a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁵ for pretrained or warm-initialized modules and 10⁻⁴ for randomly initialized ones, without warmup. Training uses bfloat16, gradient clipping at 1.0, and an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights with decay 0.999. We set σ_\min=0.05, δ=10⁻³, and λₜₑₘₚ=λ_LPIPS=0.2. Both auxiliary losses are computed in sRGB on a random 256×256 crop, with LPIPS using a VGG backbone on 4 random frames, and are weighted by ω(σ)/\max(σ,σ_\min)² with ω(σ)=(1-σ)²/((1-σ)²+κ²σ²) and κ=0.3. We drop the text prompt with probability 0.1. At inference, we clamp the guided x̂ to the valid sRGB gamut at every step, and for text-to-video generation use classifier-free guidance [28] of scale 4.0 with the default negative prompt of Wan2.1 [85]. We do not clamp in precise video editing (App. B.4), finding this produces more consistent colors.

    B.2 Text-to-Video Generation

    We train on 64K landscape videos generated by Wan2.1 at 720×1280, each with 81 frames at 16 fps and paired with its generation prompt, sampling random 21-frame windows resized and cropped to 480×832. Training takes about 57 hours, and the model totals 14.6B parameters (App. A.2).

    At evaluation, Wan2.1-T2V-14B generates 81 frames at 16 fps with its official settings (50 UniPC steps, guidance 5.0, shift 5). PixelUMM generates 96 frames at 24 fps with its released settings (35 UniPC steps, guidance 6.0, shift 10). Our models generate 21 frames at 16 fps (480×832 or 960×1664) with 50 Euler steps, guidance 4.0, and their training shifts (11 and 22). Table1 scores the first 1.3 s of every baseline video, first 21 frames for Wan2.1 and first 31 frames for PixelUMM. Table6 repeats Tab.1 with the baselines also scored over their full videos, 81 frames for Wan2.1 and 96 frames for PixelUMM. Their total scores change by at most 0.10 (84.07 and 83.82), so scoring the first 1.3 s does not favor PixVid.

    Human evaluation.

    We sample 100 random prompts from Movie Gen Video Bench [69] and generate one video per model per prompt, showing raters 21-frame, 1.3 s segments. Each pair is shown side by side in random left/right order without model names, and raters choose the better video, or a tie, for three questions: “Visual quality: Which video looks better in terms of sharpness, detail, and absence of artifacts?”, “Motion quality: Which video has more natural and smooth motion, without flickering or objects deforming?”, and “Text alignment: Which video better matches the text prompt?”. 10 raters provided 100 votes each per comparison.

    B.3 Efficient High-Resolution Generation

    Starting from Wan2.1-T2V-14B, we first train a patch-16 pixel model at 480×832 for 9K iterations (shift 11, 28 hours), and then finetune it at 960×1664 with patch 32 for 20K iterations (shift 22, 73 hours). The 39.8K training videos are generated using the captions of our text-to-video data as prompts; we sample random 21-frame windows at 24 fps, cropped and downsampled to the training resolution.

    B.4 Precise Video Editing

    Data and Training.

    The training data are 79K stock videos (74% ground-level, 26% aerial) with captions and Video Depth Anything [16] depth, as 21-frame windows at 16 fps and 480×832. The latent baseline, VACE-1.3B [43], passes both video and depth through the Wan2.1 VAE. For PixVid, we convert Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B to pixel space (20K iterations) and add VACE’s control branch, without the LPIPS loss. Both models are finetuned for 10K iterations, taking about 8 hours for PixVid and 5 for the latent model, and are sampled with the same caption and seed per clip. Per 21-frame clip, PixVid’s DiT processes 32,760 tokens per pass against the latent model’s 9,360, or 7.0× the FLOPs (28.3 vs. 4.1 PFLOPs over 100 passes, excluding the control branch). The zero-shot Wan2.1-Fun-1.3B-Control and Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control models use ZoeDepth input maps, and Cosmos-Transfer2.5 completed 962 of the 1,000 clips.

    Setup Details.

    PixVid uses patch size 16 and a four-level detailer; depth enters only through the control tokens. Both models are trained with shift 5 and a learning rate of 10⁻⁵, or 10⁻⁴ for PixVid’s newly initialized control parameters. PixVid samples with 50 Euler steps and the latent model with Wan’s default 50-step UniPC, both at shift 5. On 60 separate clips, we select the guidance scale (and, for PixVid, whether to clamp) by choosing the setting whose static-region sharpness is closest to the source among those within 3% of the lowest flow error. This yields a scale of 3 for the latent model and a scale of 2.5 without the clamp for PixVid.

    Evaluation.

    The 1,000 test clips come from 1,000 held-out videos. We split them into four bins of 250 clips each based on the 95th percentile of source optical flow, namely slow (<10.1 px/frame), moderate (10.1–29.5), medium (29.5–64.6), and fast (≥64.6). Flow is estimated with NeuFlow v2 [100]. Motion error is the end-point error between the flows of the generated and source videos, and motion kept is the ratio of their 95th-percentile flow magnitudes. Depth error is the AbsRel between Video Depth Anything estimates on the generated and source videos, aligned per clip in scale and shift. Temporal LPIPS compares the perceptual change between consecutive frames of the generated and source videos. We report medians over clips, with per-bin results in Tab.7, except for FVD and FVMD, which are set-level. FVMD uses the 962 clips completed by all models, and FVD uses all clips each model completed. PixVid has lower motion error than the finetuned latent model on 88% of fast motion clips (84% over all clips).

item.description:
一句话：循环一个共享的帧/全局注意力块，K 次细化就能换质量；训一次，旋钮在推理时调。

要点：

  • 结构：一个**循环的 transformer**，反复执行同一组共享的帧注意力与全局注意力块，并配合离散深度索引
  • 从无序图像集合直接产出逐像素射线、深度、置信度与相机位姿——不是分阶段管线
  • 关键卖点：只训练一次，细化步数 **K 变成推理时的算力旋钮**，在更小算力下匹配甚至超过大得多的前馈基线

为什么值得看：「训一次、推理时按预算调质量」是引擎里最实用的形态（对应 LOD）。多数重建模型把质量固定死在架构里，这条把它变成运行时可调的参数——对需要在不同硬件档位上跑同一套重建的团队，这个性质比刷指标更有价值。

中文摘要：Déjà View（DVLT）是 NVIDIA 等机构在 NeurIPS 2026 的 Oral 工作，实现是一套多视图三维重建的循环 transformer：它反复执行同一组共享的帧注意力和全局注意力块，并借助离散深度索引，从无序图像集合直接输出逐像素射线、深度、置信度与相机位姿。最值得引擎侧注意的性质是：模型只训练一次，而**细化步数 K 变成了推理时可控的算力旋钮**——在更小的算力下可以匹配甚至超过体量大得多的前馈基线。这相当于给重建也引入了类似 LOD 的档位概念，同一套权重适配不同硬件预算。

Déjà View: Looping Transformers for Multi-View 3D Reconstruction

NeurIPS 2026 · Oral

NVIDIAUniversity of Modena and Reggio EmiliaUniversity of TorontoETH Zurich

Alessandro Burzio*, Tobias Fischer*, Sven Elflein, Qunjie Zhou, Riccardo de Lutio, Jiawei Ren, Jiahui Huang, Shengyu Huang, Marc Pollefeys, Laura Leal-Taixé, Zan Gojcic+, Haithem Turki+

Overview

DéjàView (DVLT) is a recurrent transformer for multi-view 3D reconstruction. It loops a shared block of frame/global attention with discrete depth indexing, producing per-pixel rays, depth, confidence, and camera poses from an unordered set of images. Trained once, the number of refinement steps 

K
becomes an inference-time compute knob, matching or outperforming substantially larger feed-forward baselines at a fraction of their parameters.

This repository contains:

  • The DVLT model + four configurable ablations (vanilla, decoupled blocks, no 
    s_out
    token, no depth-scaling).
  • Evaluation wrappers for five baselines: VGGT, VGGT-Omega, Depth-Anything-3, MapAnything, and Pi3. Each wrapper imports the upstream package (installed separately — see INSTALL.md).
  • A training stack built on 
    accelerate
    + Hydra, with optional W&B logging.
  • A Stage-2 fine-tune recipe for the depth-conv head.
  • Rerun-based visualization tools.

    • Release status

  • Inference code
  • Model weights
  • Evaluation code
  • eval datasets preprocess and loaders
  • Training code
  • ScanNet++ training dataset loader
  • other training dataset loaders

    • Quickstart

    Install

    See docs/INSTALL.md. The short version:

    conda create -n dvlt python=3.12 && conda activate dvlt
conda install pytorch=2.5.1 torchvision pytorch-cuda=12.4 -c pytorch -c nvidia -c conda-forge
pip install -e .[all]

    Quick setup

    Quick example script:

    import torch
from accelerate import Accelerator

from dvlt.model.dvlt.model import DVLT
from dvlt.util.preprocess import load_sequence, preprocess_images

checkpoint_path = "nvidia/dvlt"  # local dir, HTTPS URL, or HF Hub repo id
# load_sequence accepts a directory, a single video, or an explicit list of files.
input_path = "path/to/scene_dir"
# Or: input_path = "path/to/clip.mp4"
# Or: from glob import glob; input_path = sorted(glob("path/to/scene_dir/*.png"))

accelerator = Accelerator(mixed_precision="bf16")

model = DVLT(img_size=504)
model.load_pretrained(checkpoint_path, strict=True)
model.setup_test(accelerator)

_, frames = load_sequence(input_path)
batch = preprocess_images(frames, img_size=504, patch_size=14, device=accelerator.device)

with torch.no_grad(), accelerator.autocast():
    predictions = model.predict(batch, accelerator)

cameras = predictions["cameras"][0]            # Cameras object with shape [S]
extrinsics_c2w = cameras.camera_to_worlds       # (S, 3, 4) — OpenCV convention [R | t]
intrinsics = cameras.get_intrinsics_matrices()  # (S, 3, 3)

depths = predictions["depths"][0]              # (S, H, W)
world_points = predictions["world_points"][0]  # (S, H, W, 3)

    # Single-GPU
python -m dvlt.scripts.train --config-name dvlt-large data=scannetpp

# Resume
python -m dvlt.scripts.train \
    --config-dir=outputs/ \
    --config-name=config.yaml \
    trainer.resume_from_checkpoint=latest

item.title: 少步蒸馏的假模型被「中间态」带偏：eDMD 只看端点分布，让匹配方向不再被中间步污染 ｜ eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
item.description:
一句话：已有的 DMD 在多步蒸馏时训练假模型的信号里混进了中间分布，方向被扭曲。

要点：

  • 机制回顾：分布匹配蒸馏（DMD）用一个辅助的 **fake score 模型**追踪学生分布，再用教师与假预测之间的差驱动学生靠向教师
  • 问题定位：多步蒸馏中学生只交付最终输出，但现有方法却在**中间状态或全部去噪步**上训练假模型，导致更新信号与中间分布纠缠
  • 后果很具体：匹配方向被扭曲，而且当学生的最终输出已经对齐教师时，这个信号仍然非零；eDMD 因此改为只做**端点**分布匹配

为什么值得看：少步蒸馏是压实时生成成本的主力手段，而「信号还剩多少噪声」直接决定学生能到多好。把匹配目标从全轨迹收回到端点，是那种「改一行目标函数、白拿质量」的工程胜利。

中文摘要：分布匹配蒸馏（DMD）是少步扩散蒸馏的主流范式：它用一个辅助的 fake score 模型追踪学生模型当前的分布，再用教师与假预测之间的差异把学生推向教师。但在多步蒸馏里，学生最终只交付一个输出，而现有方法却在中间状态或全部去噪步上训练假模型，于是学生的更新信号与中间分布纠缠在一起：匹配方向会被扭曲，并且当学生的最终输出已经与教师对齐时，这个信号依然不等于零。eDMD 因此把匹配限制在**端点分布**上，让监督只反映「最终结果像不像」，从而拿回更干净的更新方向。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-13

本期推送：2026-11-15

eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation

Abstract

Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student’s distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student’s final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student’s update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student’s final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student’s final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student’s final output distribution matches the teacher’s, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

††footnotetext: †Corresponding author: chizhang@westlake.edu.cn.

1 Introduction

Diffusion and flow matching models have achieved remarkable success in high-quality image [10, 6], video [50], and audio [22] generation. However, their iterative sampling processes typically require tens of network evaluations, resulting in substantial inference costs. Few-step distillation addresses this limitation by transferring the generative capabilities of a pretrained teacher into a student that requires only one or a few denoising steps [44, 49, 40, 19]. Among existing approaches, distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as one of the most effective and widely adopted paradigms [33, 62]. While DMD has demonstrated impressive one-step generation capabilities, a single network evaluation often struggles to preserve fine-grained details and complex structures [61]. Recent methods therefore extend DMD to multi-step generation, allowing the student to progressively refine its predictions and achieve higher generation quality while maintaining efficient inference [61, 34, 21, 23].

The central idea of DMD is to train the student by minimizing the distributional discrepancy between its generated samples and those of the pretrained teacher. Specifically, DMD formulates this objective through the reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between their noise-perturbed distributions, whose gradient can be estimated from the difference between the teacher’s and student’s score functions [62]. Since the student’s score is not directly available, DMD introduces an auxiliary diffusion model, known as the fake score model, which is trained online on student-generated samples to approximate the student’s distribution. The discrepancy between the teacher’s prediction, often enhanced with classifier-free guidance (CFG) [9], and the fake model’s estimate then provides the correction signal for updating the student. Importantly, the distribution learned by the fake model determines the reference against which the student is optimized. When denoising is performed in a single step, the student’s prediction is also its final generated output, making the distribution learned by the fake model naturally consistent with the desired matching objective. When denoising involves multiple steps, however, the student produces a sequence of intermediate predictions before generating its final output. These predictions generally follow different distributions, so how the fake model is trained becomes a central design choice.

Existing multi-step DMD methods incorporate intermediate predictions or states into the training of the fake model (Fig.2), following two paradigms. The first, represented by DMD2 [61], trains a shared fake model using predictions collected from different denoising steps, effectively learning a mixture of intermediate and final prediction distributions. The second, represented by TDM [34], constructs stage-dependent references from intermediate denoising states and performs distribution matching within their corresponding noise intervals. Despite their different implementations, both paradigms couple the distribution matching objective to intermediate distributions, whereas the ultimate goal of distillation is to match the student’s final output distribution to the teacher’s. This distinction is particularly important for few-step students, which compress a complex generative process into only a few steps. Their intermediate predictions need not follow the teacher’s corresponding distributions, even when their final outputs accurately reproduce the teacher’s distribution. Therefore, imposing distributional constraints on intermediate predictions may introduce unnecessary restrictions and interfere with the optimization of final generation quality.

To understand the consequences of this mismatch, we theoretically analyze how the fake model’s reference distribution influences the student update. We denote the distribution of the student’s final outputs as the endpoint distribution. Under exact conditional denoisers, we decompose the DMD correction signal into three components (Eq.3): a teacher enhancement term arising from guidance, an endpoint matching term that measures the discrepancy between the teacher and the student’s final output distribution, and an additional reference residual caused by the discrepancy between the fake model’s reference distribution and the endpoint distribution. Our analysis reveals that existing intermediate-based references can introduce a nonzero residual that fundamentally changes the intended distribution matching behavior. Even when the student’s final output distribution already matches the teacher’s, this residual may remain nonzero and continue to push the student away from the desired distribution. We further prove that the reference residual vanishes if and only if the fake model represents the endpoint distribution, regardless of the student’s intermediate distributions (Prop.1). Our two-dimensional synthetic experiments confirm these effects, showing that intermediate-based references deflect the update from the desired direction, whereas an endpoint-aligned reference does not (Fig.3).

These findings motivate a simple principle: the fake model should represent the distribution of the samples that distillation ultimately aims to optimize, rather than the intermediate predictions used to generate them. Based on this principle, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student’s final generated outputs and uses it to provide correction signals for every denoising step. By aligning the fake model’s reference with the endpoint distribution, eDMD eliminates the reference residual and ensures that the distribution matching signal is determined by the discrepancy between the teacher and the student’s final outputs, independently of the intermediate sampling trajectory (Corollary1). This allows intermediate steps to take whatever form best suits few-step generation, without imposing unnecessary distributional constraints.

Beyond correcting the student-side distribution reference, effective DMD also depends on the quality of the supervision provided by the teacher. D-DMD [21] identifies CFG augmentation of the teacher prediction as the primary engine of few-step distillation. However, existing methods typically obtain teacher targets through a single guided network evaluation at each sampled noise level. Such predictions can average over multiple plausible outputs and lose fine-grained details, whereas the teacher achieves high-quality generation through iterative denoising (Fig.2, bottom). To improve the precision of teacher supervision, we introduce a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step teacher predictions with short multi-step guided trajectories within the final denoising interval, providing sharper and more accurate supervision without increasing student inference cost. Furthermore, teacher predictions are not equally reliable across noise levels, as guidance and model approximation errors can introduce inconsistencies between predictions at different noise levels. Uniformly sampling noise levels may therefore expose intermediate student steps to unreliable supervision. To address this issue, we introduce a calibrated query density that estimates the teacher’s cross-level prediction consistency before distillation and concentrates intermediate-step queries on noise levels that provide more reliable supervision.

Overall, eDMD aligns the distribution matching objective with the student’s final outputs and improves the quality of teacher supervision. We evaluate eDMD on four representative diffusion and flow matching backbones (SD3-Medium [6], FLUX.2-klein-4B, FLUX.2-klein-9B [2], and Qwen-Image-2.1 [38]), distilling each into a 4-step generator without using real images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching baselines, achieving the highest peak HPSv3++ [26] scores across all four backbones. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We identify and theoretically characterize an objective mismatch in multi-step DMD: training the fake model on intermediate predictions introduces a reference residual that distorts distribution matching and vanishes if and only if the fake model learns the endpoint distribution.

  • •

    We propose eDMD, which trains a shared fake model exclusively on the student’s final outputs and strengthens teacher supervision through a multi-step precise teacher (PT) and a calibrated query density.

  • •

    Experiments on four backbones show consistent improvements over existing distribution matching methods, with higher human-preference scores, improved fine-grained details, and fewer structural artifacts.

    • 2 Related work

    Few-step diffusion distillation. Few-step distillation trains a student to match the quality of a diffusion or flow matching teacher [10, 48, 20] in only a few sampling steps. Trajectory-based methods train the student to follow the teacher’s sampling path: progressive distillation merges adjacent steps [44, 36], rectified flows straighten the path [24, 25], and consistency and flow-map methods learn direct mappings from noisy states to cleaner states [49, 32, 15, 52, 40, 29, 41]. Adversarial methods instead align output distributions using a discriminator against real or teacher samples [46, 45, 19]. Distribution matching, which our work builds upon, aligns them using score estimates from the teacher and an online fake model.

    Distribution matching distillation. Building on score distillation for text-to-3D generation [37, 55], Diff-Instruct and DMD update the student with the score difference between the pretrained teacher and a fake model trained online on the student’s samples [33, 62]. Subsequent work explores alternative divergences [65, 60, 54], incorporates adversarial objectives [61, 31], refines the fake score estimate or the update direction [7, 58], or mitigates mode collapse [56, 18]. DMD2 extends DMD to multi-step generation [61], a setting adopted by many later methods [21, 23, 34, 66, 27, 56]. Their fake models are typically trained on intermediate predictions or states, whereas we show that only a fake model trained on final outputs avoids biasing the student update. This also explains a choice found in some implementations: ADM fits its fake model to final outputs in its training algorithm [31], and the final-step matching variant of SiD supervises only the final output by back-propagating through the entire sampling chain [66], whereas eDMD corrects every step directly.

    Teacher supervision. Distillation relies on the quality of the teacher’s supervision. For diffusion models, generation quality often depends on guidance, from CFG [9] and its refinements [17, 53, 42] to guidance by a weaker model [14] or by perturbed attention [1]. D-DMD shows that the same holds in DMD: CFG augmentation of the teacher prediction is the primary engine of few-step distillation, with distribution matching acting as a regularizer [21]. Strengthening the teacher’s supervision is therefore a direct way to improve the student, for example by fine-tuning the teacher [34], targeting a reward-tilted teacher distribution [13], or deriving regression targets from the teacher’s own denoising outputs [68, 46, 8, 56].

    3 Reference distribution of the fake model

    We now analyze how the distribution that the fake model is trained on, which we call its reference distribution, shapes the student update in multi-step DMD.

    3.1 Multi-step distribution matching

    Distribution matching. DMD trains a student to match a pretrained teacher’s distribution [62]. We first consider a single-step student that generates samples x̂∼q in ℝⁿ, and write p for the teacher distribution. DMD minimizes the reverse KL divergence between their noise-perturbed distributions q_τ and p_τ, where samples are perturbed as y=(1-τ)x+τε at level τ∈(0,1), with ε∼ℕ(0,Iₙ)[24, 6]. For a distribution r, let Dᵣ(y,τ) denote its denoiser, i.e., the prediction of a diffusion model trained on r: the average clean sample given the noisy sample y. The gradient with respect to the student parameters θ is

    ∇_θ KL(q_τ ∥ p_τ)(1)
    =-(1-τ)²/τ² 𝔼[(Dₚ(y,τ)-D_q(y,τ)) (∂x̂)/(∂θ)].

    The student is thus moved along the difference between two denoisers: Dₚ is given by the teacher, and D_q is estimated by a fake model F trained online on the student’s samples.

    Multi-step students. While one-step generation is efficient, a single network evaluation often struggles to preserve fine-grained details and complex structures. Multi-step students address this limitation by progressively refining their predictions over a few denoising steps [61]. A K-step student G_θ starts from pure noise z₀ and follows a noise grid 1=σ₀>…>σ_K=0. At step k=0,…,K-1, it moves from state zₖ to zₖ₊₁ and provides a clean predictionx̂ₖ, an estimate of the clean sample given zₖ. At the last step, this prediction coincides with the final output z_K. We denote the prediction distributions by qₖ and the final output distribution by q, the endpoint distribution.

    Multi-step update. During multi-step DMD training, we select a step k and construct a noisy input y from its clean prediction x̂ₖ or its resulting state zₖ₊₁. This input and its noise level τ form a query to the teacher and fake model. Denoting their predictions by A(y,τ) and F(y,τ), respectively, we use the difference C=A-F to correct x̂ₖ through the surrogate loss [62, 61]

    L_G=𝔼 ∥x̂ₖ-sg[x̂ₖ+C/ω]∥²,

    		(2)

    where sg stops gradients and ω=∥x̂ₖ-A∥₁/n is the mean absolute difference over the sample’s n coordinates. The teacher target A is often obtained by enhancing Dₚ with guidance such as CFG [9]. The fake model F is trained online on selected student samples. We denote their distribution by ν and call it the reference distribution.

    Decomposing the correction. To understand how the fake model’s training distribution affects this update, assume an exact fake model, F=D_ν. Adding and subtracting the teacher denoiser Dₚ and the endpoint denoiser D_q gives

    C=(A-Dₚ) (teacher enhancement)+(Dₚ-D_q) (endpoint matching)+(D_q-D_ν) (reference residualR).

    		(3)

    The teacher enhancement strengthens teacher supervision, for example through CFG [21]. The endpoint matching term is the distribution matching direction for the student’s final outputs, as in Eq.1. The reference residualR is the extra correction caused by a mismatch between the fake reference and the student’s endpoint distribution.

    3.2 The reference residual

    Proposition 1(Reference residual).

    Assume exact conditional denoisers under a shared forward noising process. At every noise level 0<τ<1,

    R=D_q-D_ν=τ²/1-τ ∇_y\log(q_τ)/(ν_τ),

Abstract

Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student’s distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student’s final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student’s update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student’s final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student’s final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student’s final output distribution matches the teacher’s, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

1 Introduction

Diffusion and flow matching models have achieved remarkable success in high-quality image [10, 6], video [50], and audio [22] generation. However, their iterative sampling processes typically require tens of network evaluations, resulting in substantial inference costs. Few-step distillation addresses this limitation by transferring the generative capabilities of a pretrained teacher into a student that requires only one or a few denoising steps [44, 49, 40, 19]. Among existing approaches, distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as one of the most effective and widely adopted paradigms [33, 62]. While DMD has demonstrated impressive one-step generation capabilities, a single network evaluation often struggles to preserve fine-grained details and complex structures [61]. Recent methods therefore extend DMD to multi-step generation, allowing the student to progressively refine its predictions and achieve higher generation quality while maintaining efficient inference [61, 34, 21, 23].

The central idea of DMD is to train the student by minimizing the distributional discrepancy between its generated samples and those of the pretrained teacher. Specifically, DMD formulates this objective through the reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between their noise-perturbed distributions, whose gradient can be estimated from the difference between the teacher’s and student’s score functions [62]. Since the student’s score is not directly available, DMD introduces an auxiliary diffusion model, known as the fake score model, which is trained online on student-generated samples to approximate the student’s distribution. The discrepancy between the teacher’s prediction, often enhanced with classifier-free guidance (CFG) [9], and the fake model’s estimate then provides the correction signal for updating the student. Importantly, the distribution learned by the fake model determines the reference against which the student is optimized. When denoising is performed in a single step, the student’s prediction is also its final generated output, making the distribution learned by the fake model naturally consistent with the desired matching objective. When denoising involves multiple steps, however, the student produces a sequence of intermediate predictions before generating its final output. These predictions generally follow different distributions, so how the fake model is trained becomes a central design choice.

Existing multi-step DMD methods incorporate intermediate predictions or states into the training of the fake model (Fig.2), following two paradigms. The first, represented by DMD2 [61], trains a shared fake model using predictions collected from different denoising steps, effectively learning a mixture of intermediate and final prediction distributions. The second, represented by TDM [34], constructs stage-dependent references from intermediate denoising states and performs distribution matching within their corresponding noise intervals. Despite their different implementations, both paradigms couple the distribution matching objective to intermediate distributions, whereas the ultimate goal of distillation is to match the student’s final output distribution to the teacher’s. This distinction is particularly important for few-step students, which compress a complex generative process into only a few steps. Their intermediate predictions need not follow the teacher’s corresponding distributions, even when their final outputs accurately reproduce the teacher’s distribution. Therefore, imposing distributional constraints on intermediate predictions may introduce unnecessary restrictions and interfere with the optimization of final generation quality.

To understand the consequences of this mismatch, we theoretically analyze how the fake model’s reference distribution influences the student update. We denote the distribution of the student’s final outputs as the endpoint distribution. Under exact conditional denoisers, we decompose the DMD correction signal into three components (Eq.3): a teacher enhancement term arising from guidance, an endpoint matching term that measures the discrepancy between the teacher and the student’s final output distribution, and an additional reference residual caused by the discrepancy between the fake model’s reference distribution and the endpoint distribution. Our analysis reveals that existing intermediate-based references can introduce a nonzero residual that fundamentally changes the intended distribution matching behavior. Even when the student’s final output distribution already matches the teacher’s, this residual may remain nonzero and continue to push the student away from the desired distribution. We further prove that the reference residual vanishes if and only if the fake model represents the endpoint distribution, regardless of the student’s intermediate distributions (Prop.1). Our two-dimensional synthetic experiments confirm these effects, showing that intermediate-based references deflect the update from the desired direction, whereas an endpoint-aligned reference does not (Fig.3).

These findings motivate a simple principle: the fake model should represent the distribution of the samples that distillation ultimately aims to optimize, rather than the intermediate predictions used to generate them. Based on this principle, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student’s final generated outputs and uses it to provide correction signals for every denoising step. By aligning the fake model’s reference with the endpoint distribution, eDMD eliminates the reference residual and ensures that the distribution matching signal is determined by the discrepancy between the teacher and the student’s final outputs, independently of the intermediate sampling trajectory (Corollary1). This allows intermediate steps to take whatever form best suits few-step generation, without imposing unnecessary distributional constraints.

Beyond correcting the student-side distribution reference, effective DMD also depends on the quality of the supervision provided by the teacher. D-DMD [21] identifies CFG augmentation of the teacher prediction as the primary engine of few-step distillation. However, existing methods typically obtain teacher targets through a single guided network evaluation at each sampled noise level. Such predictions can average over multiple plausible outputs and lose fine-grained details, whereas the teacher achieves high-quality generation through iterative denoising (Fig.2, bottom). To improve the precision of teacher supervision, we introduce a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step teacher predictions with short multi-step guided trajectories within the final denoising interval, providing sharper and more accurate supervision without increasing student inference cost. Furthermore, teacher predictions are not equally reliable across noise levels, as guidance and model approximation errors can introduce inconsistencies between predictions at different noise levels. Uniformly sampling noise levels may therefore expose intermediate student steps to unreliable supervision. To address this issue, we introduce a calibrated query density that estimates the teacher’s cross-level prediction consistency before distillation and concentrates intermediate-step queries on noise levels that provide more reliable supervision.

Overall, eDMD aligns the distribution matching objective with the student’s final outputs and improves the quality of teacher supervision.
